sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Stabilization of Severe Anaphylaxis
sections.description: This section establishes the foundational clinical picture of the case, detailing the patient's demographics, comorbidities, and the acute presentation of anaphylactic shock triggered by clarithromycin. It outlines the immediate recognition of life-threatening symptoms (hypotension, hypoxia, cutaneous signs) and the execution of standard emergency stabilization protocols, highlighting the critical role of epinephrine and supportive care.
subtopics: Patient profile: Comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension), medication history, and prior allergic events
Trigger identification: Clarithromycin ingestion vs. prior clindamycin rash
Acute symptomatology: Progression from pruritus to hemodynamic collapse (BP 74/50 mmHg) and hypoxia
Initial emergency interventions: IM epinephrine (auto-injector limitations), IV fluids, oxygen therapy, and antihistamines
Immediate clinical response: Resolution of shock and transition to inpatient monitoring

sections.section_title: The Challenge of Multiphasic Courses: Definition and Diagnostic Reasoning
sections.description: Focusing on the core complexity of the case—the recurrence of symptoms—this section distinguishes between monophasic, biphasic, and multiphasic anaphylaxis. It explores the diagnostic dilemma faced by clinicians in differentiating true relapse from refractory anaphylaxis or incomplete allergen clearance, while reviewing current epidemiological data and the variability in definition across guidelines.
subtopics: Defining multiphasic anaphylaxis vs. biphasic reactions vs. refractory anaphylaxis
Timeline analysis: Recurrence patterns within the first 12 hours post-stabilization
Differential diagnosis considerations: Ruling out ongoing allergen absorption or secondary causes
Epidemiology: Incidence rates (0.4%–23%) and lack of standardized prediction models
Risk stratification challenges: Identifying high-risk features in this specific patient

sections.section_title: Management Strategies for Recurrent Episodes and Therapeutic Dilemmas
sections.description: This section details the iterative management decisions made during the patient's four separate anaphylactic episodes. It critically evaluates treatment modifications, including escalating epinephrine dosages (from 0.3 mg to 0.5 mg), the controversial role of corticosteroids in preventing recurrence, and the consideration versus rejection of continuous IV epinephrine infusion based on evolving symptom severity.
subtopics: Epinephrine dosing nuances: Auto-injector (0.3 mg) inadequacy vs. guideline-recommended 0.5 mg in adults >50 kg
Escalation strategy: Transitioning from auto-injectors to manually prepared higher-dose IM injections
Corticosteroid debate: Historical rationale for prevention vs. modern evidence regarding efficacy and harm
Advanced therapeutic options analyzed: Continuous IV epinephrine infusion vs. expectant management
**Clinical Course**: Symptom attenuation pattern across four distinct episodes
